package.intro: Attila ruled the Huns for less than twenty years, but in that time he squeezed thousands of pounds of gold out of Rome, ravaged the Balkans, Gaul and Italy, and became a byword for destruction. This documentary tells his story, and explains how much of it comes from his enemies.
facts: The Huns arrived in eastern Europe around 370, pushing the Goths into the Roman Empire
Attila and his brother Bleda inherited the Hunnic kingdom from their uncle Rugila around 434
The peace of 443 raised the Eastern Roman tribute to 2,100 pounds of gold a year
Bleda died around 445, according to Roman sources killed by Attila
The Roman diplomat Priscus visited Attila's court in 449 and left an eyewitness account
Attila invaded Gaul in 451 and was checked by Aetius and the Visigoths at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
Invaded Italy and destroyed Aquileia in 452, then withdrew after meeting an embassy including Pope Leo I
Died in 453 after his wedding to Ildico; the Huns were defeated by their former subjects at Nedao in 454
package.sources: Priscus of Panium (fragments); Jordanes, Getica (c. 551); Encyclopaedia Britannica; Peter Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire; Christopher Kelly, Attila the Hun: Barbarian Terror and the Fall of the Roman Empire; E. A. Thompson, The Huns.

sections.name: Cold open
lines: In the summer of 449, a Roman diplomat named Priscus rode north across the Danube into the lands of the Huns, to meet the most feared man in Europe.
He found him at a feast in a wooden hall. The guests ate from silver plates and drank from gold cups. Their host, Attila, used a plain wooden cup and wore simple clothes.
By then, the Eastern Roman Empire was paying him two thousand one hundred pounds of gold every year, simply to be left alone.
Later Christian writers called him the Scourge of God, a punishment sent from heaven. Yet he ruled for less than twenty years, and his empire vanished almost as soon as he died.

sections.name: Out of the steppe
lines: The Huns were nomadic horsemen from the steppes of central Asia. Exactly where they came from is still debated. They were superb mounted archers.
Around 370, they burst into eastern Europe, driving the Goths before them. Fleeing Goths crossed into the Roman Empire, setting off a chain of events that shook Rome to its foundations.
By the 420s, the Huns had settled on the great plain of what is now Hungary. Rome sometimes fought them, and sometimes hired them as mercenaries.

lines.place: Hunnic lands · north of the Danube

lines: Attila was probably born around 406. Almost nothing is known of his childhood. His uncle, Rugila, ruled the Huns.

sections.name: Two brothers
lines: When Rugila died, around 434, Attila and his elder brother, Bleda, inherited his kingdom together.

lines.title: Treaty of Margus
lines: Tribute doubled: 700 lb gold a year
They quickly forced the Eastern Roman Empire, ruled from Constantinople, into a treaty that doubled its yearly payment to them, to seven hundred pounds of gold.
When the Romans fell behind, the brothers invaded the Balkans. Cities such as Naissus, the modern Niš in Serbia, were stormed and sacked.

lines.label: gold a year demanded from Constantinople · 443

lines: The peace that followed tripled the tribute to two thousand one hundred pounds of gold a year, plus six thousand pounds in arrears.
Around 445, Bleda died. Roman writers say Attila had him killed. From then on, he ruled alone.

sections.name: The court of Attila

lines.name: Attila
lines.role: King of the Huns. Ruled with Bleda from c. 434, alone from c. 445.

lines: Priscus described him as short and broad-chested, with a large head, small deep-set eyes, and a thin beard flecked with grey.
Priscus watched him sit outside his hall, judging disputes brought to him by his people. His followers treated him with a mixture of devotion and fear.
His empire was not only Huns. It included Germanic peoples such as the Ostrogoths and Gepids, and many others, held together by loyalty, fear and a share of the plunder.
In 447, he struck the Balkans again, reaching as far south as Thermopylae in Greece. Constantinople's great walls, hastily repaired after an earthquake, kept him out of the capital.

lines.text: A Roman official plotted to have Attila murdered. Attila found out.

lines: The Romans tried another way. While Priscus's embassy was at the Hun court, a senior Roman official was secretly plotting to have Attila assassinated. Attila found out, and sent envoys to shame the emperor.

sections.name: Gaul
lines: Then, in 450, came an extraordinary message. Honoria, sister of the Western Roman emperor, Valentinian, was being pushed into a marriage she did not want. She sent Attila her ring and a plea for help.

lines.text: Half the Western Empire as a dowry

lines: Attila chose to treat it as a marriage proposal. He demanded Honoria as his bride, and half of the Western Empire as her dowry.
Valentinian was furious. Honoria was married off to someone else, and Attila had his excuse for war.
In 451, he crossed the Rhine into Gaul, modern France, with a huge army. Cities such as Metz were sacked, and Orléans was besieged.

lines.name: Flavius Aetius
lines.role: Roman general. Had lived among the Huns as a young hostage.

lines: Against him stood Flavius Aetius, the Western Empire's leading general. As a young man, Aetius had lived among the Huns as a hostage, and knew them well.
Aetius allied with the Visigoths, a Germanic people settled in southern Gaul. In the summer of 451, the two sides met at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains.
It was one of the bloodiest battles of the age, and the Visigothic king, Theodoric, was killed. A later historian claimed a hundred and sixty-five thousand died, surely an exaggeration.
Attila was forced to retreat, but his army survived. Aetius let him go, perhaps wanting the Huns to remain as a counterweight to the Visigoths.

sections.name: Italy
lines: The next year, he invaded Italy. After a long siege, the city of Aquileia, near the head of the Adriatic, was destroyed so thoroughly that it never fully recovered.
Refugees fled to the islands of the nearby lagoons. Later tradition linked them to the founding of Venice.

lines.name: Pope Leo I
lines.role: Met Attila in northern Italy in 452. Soon after, Attila turned back.

lines: Milan and other cities fell. Then an embassy from Rome came to meet him, including Pope Leo the First. Soon afterwards, Attila turned back.
Christian legend credited the pope. Historians also point to famine in Italy, disease in the Hun army, and an Eastern Roman attack on the Huns' homeland.

sections.name: Death
lines: Early in 453, Attila took another wife, a young woman named Ildico. After the wedding feast, he went to bed drunk.
The next day, his attendants broke down the door and found him dead, his bride weeping beside him.
According to Priscus, as retold by the Gothic historian Jordanes, he had suffered a severe nosebleed in his sleep and choked. Later rumours blamed his bride.

lines.text: Buried in coffins of gold, silver and iron; the gravediggers were killed.

lines: Jordanes adds that he was buried at night in three coffins, of gold, silver and iron, and that the men who buried him were killed to keep the place secret. His grave has never been found.

sections.name: Collapse
lines: His sons fought over his empire. In 454, the subject peoples, led by Ardaric, king of the Gepids, rose up and defeated the Huns at the Battle of Nedao.
Aetius did not outlive Attila by long. In 454, the emperor Valentinian killed him in the palace. Twenty-two years later, the Western Roman Empire itself was gone.
One of his sons, Dengizich, kept fighting the Romans. In 469 he was killed, and his head was displayed in Constantinople.
Within about fifteen years of Attila's death, the Hunnic empire had disappeared.

sections.name: Legacy

lines.head: Etzel and Atli
lines.sub: Attila in German and Norse epic

lines: Attila lived on in legend. In the German epic, the Nibelungenlied, he appears as Etzel, a fairly mild king. In Norse sagas, he is Atli, a greedy tyrant.
In Hungary, where his empire was centred, he is remembered more kindly, and Attila is still a common boy's name.

He left no buildings, laws or writings. Everything we know comes from enemies who feared him. Modern historians see a shrewd ruler who understood Rome's weaknesses, and preferred extorting gold to conquering land.

lines.text: A name that outlived its empire

lines: Attila built nothing that lasted. His empire was a machine for taking gold and plunder, and it fell apart within a generation. What survived was the fear, and his name.
